Mr. Chairman, it is not my intention tonight to make a lengthy or detailed analysis of the department. After all, we are dealing with last year's estimates which to a large extent have been passed. We have a new minister, and I hope that in the near future this year's estimates will go before the standing committee which will be able to give the minister and the department the kind of searching examination that I think is long overdue.
I must say I was disappointed in the very general statement which the minister made. I had expected and I still expect some very excellent leadership from the minister. But I must tell him that the kind of speech he made has been made by every minister of citizenship and immigration appointed since I came to the house.
March 7, 1966

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration
Talking of ministers of citizenship and immigration, I could not help but be struck by the speech of the hon. member for Carleton, a former minister. What he said in effect, in his speech was: "Do as I say, but don't do as I did". If there was one thing which was characteristic of immigration policy while the hon. member for Carleton was minister, and also the minister who preceded him, it was the fact that they did not clear up any of the basic problems which the department faced then and still faces now. While I have not the figures here and do not want to precipitate a long and acrimonious debate on this department, the fact is that in the years in which the former government was in power we had some of the lowest rates of immigration that we have had in the last 25 years.
This was because to a large extent, I suppose, we had large scale unemployment. Naturally when you have large scale unemployment the people who have to work for a living are sometimes not too happy about immigration. They look on immigrants as prospective competitors for jobs. The way to get the co-operation of labour is to have full employment. Then the working people do not worry about immigrants who come to Canada and compete for jobs.
The tide has turned. Immigration figures are now up but not up to the level which, I suppose, many members would like to see. I think this is partly due to the fact that in Europe and those countries to which we have traditionally looked for immigrants there has been full employment for about the last ten years. Up until this year Canada had pretty heavy unemployment while Great Britain, Germany, the Scandinavian countries, Holland and Belgium were experiencing prosperity with full employment. Therefore it has not been too easy to encourage people from those countries from which we have traditionally received the bulk of our immigrants. We have had to turn, and we have turned with some success, to countries such as Greece and Portugal for our immigrants.
I am not being critical in this regard. I think we ought to open the gates to immigrants from many countries who in past years we have seemed to discourage. But I am concerned about the fact that morally, and I think even legally, it is the responsibility of the federal government to bring people here. After all, the federal government encourages them to come to Canada. It is the federal government which has immigration offices in most countries in Europe, the

Middle East and Asia. It is the federal government which informs these people of the kind of living they can expect here. Yet having brought them here and encouraged them to come, once they arrive to a large extent they are forgotten.
I have before me an editorial which appeared in the Toronto Globe and Mail for February 18,	1966 entitled "Victims Of
Language". It reads in part as follows:
An informal survey of Toronto secondary schools has uncovered evidence that immigrant children with language difficulties are being encouraged to leave school.
Then the editorial goes on to say a little further on:
As a consequence, hundreds, perhaps thousands, of boys and girls, many of them of university calibre, are succumbing to pressures to drop out. Whether the pressure originates in the family or in the school, whether it is overt or implicit, is immaterial. The fact remains that they are being denied the opportunities of a full education.
The editorial concludes by stating that the provincial and municipal governments have a responsibility to see that this kind of thing does not happen.
I suggest to the minister and the government that the federal government has a responsibility in this regard. I am not going to minimize the difficulties which are created for the federal government by the fact that education is the responsibility of the provinces and I am not suggesting at this time that this situation should change. But I do suggest to the minister that if in its wisdom, and I think with the agreement of the Economic Council of Canada as well as business, industry and labour, the federal government believes that we need an aggressive and active policy of immigration and that we need to encourage people from countries in which the mother tongue is neither English nor French to come to Canada, then it must somehow find ways to help the young people who accompany their parents and who are not fully conversant with the English language to overcome their language deficiency. If we do not do so then these people will become the future unemployed, the future poverty cases, the people who will inevitably become a charge on the state in generations to come.
I suggest that the minister might well look into this matter now. As one of the ways of combating poverty in the war on poverty, which so far has really been a war of words, the government might consider co-operating with the provincial governments in this respect.

There are a few points, Mr. Chairman, on which I would like to dwell in reply to questions. First of all, there is one that struck me and I should like hon. members to understand that their words touched me. It is the issue of discrimination in immigration. Undoubtedly, discriminatory provisions remain in the act, and I believe there will shortly be means to eliminate such discrimination in a democratic country like ours.
There are historical reasons for that. Doubtless, many historical reasons explain the situation, but I feel the past should be obliterated and we in Canada should be in a position to accept immigrants whatever the colour of their skin, their religion their race and their language. That is basic.
Now, I believe it was the hon. member for Carleton who referred to a general immigration policy, that is that policy which is to be adjusted on a short term basis, as opposed to a long term one that would take into account the normal, gradual and continuous development of Canada.
On this point, I am in complete agreement with the hon. member for Carleton. Our policy cannot be a short term one, because then it easily becomes absurd. Since we do not know about the short term movements and can hardly forecast them, as the hon. member said, we spend our time opening and shutting the tap; but since our forecasts were wrong, the tap is always opened or shut at the wrong time.
Therefore, I think that we will have to disregard those short term movements and try to elaborate a policy-I am not saying that we will not make mistakes-which will at least be a little more in agreement with our ideas and our views about the future of Canada.
The hon. member for Nicolet-Yamaska (Mr. Vincent) talked about immigration. He touched upon a sensitive subject, in view of the ethnic composition of Canada, namely immigration from France or French speaking countries compared to immigration which might come from other countries, such as England.

That is a problem which exists in Canada and it might be better to talk about it since it exists.
There is no doubt that our facilities are much better in England than in France as far as personnel and offices are concerned.
But, in spite of that, it remains that France is still a country which does not favour immigration, and the French people themselves do not emigrate easily, especially at this time because there is full employment in France.

We have improved our offices in Portugal. I think that last year immigration from Portugal increased considerably; it might increase again during the current year.

I think that very soon, and I hope that it will be within a few weeks-that depends of course on the house because it might also be in a few months if incidents such as those we witnessed today and last week should happen-we will be able to deal with this situation under which visiting Canada has now become a normal means of coming as an immigrant.

But, at the present time, there is no doubt that many people who come to Canada to stay come as visitors, because it is easier or because we do not have in their mother countries facilities where they can pass the required examinations before coming to Canada.

He said that, traditionally, the Department of Labour has been opposed to immigration. What he meant, no doubt-and he may correct me if I am wrong-is that this stems from the influence exerted by labour unions on the Department of Labour which has been rather conservative in the field of immigration.
It is a fact that labour unions are conservative in this respect.

I know of no labour unions in Canada that would oppose immigration, provided that there is no increase, through immigration, in the number of unemployed on the Canadian labour market.
Therefore, I believe that so long as we have a normal employment situation, there is nothing to fear from the labour movement; they will agree to immigrants coming to enrich the economic and cultural life of Canada.


Therefore, this is a matter of maintaining a proper balance, but it is obvious that Canada needs qualified labour, and emphasis should be placed on this. Mr. Chairman, I am only going to raise two matters at this time relating to questions of citizenship and immigration that are involved when a person becomes a citizen. In the first place, I think we all agree that a person in applying to become a

naturalized citizen is really showing an expression of faith in that he wants to become part of this country and become one, with the rest of us. Such an application is an expression of faith because it is voluntary and because it is not a requirement. Because of that I think we are somewhat rigid in maintaining the five year residence requirement. The period of five years may have had some value in the past even though then, as now, it was an arbitrary figure. I know of many people who have come to Canada in recent years who are patiently and sometimes impatiently waiting for the day when the five years of residence will be up so that they can make an application to become Canadian citizens. There would be no difference whatever in their value to themselves, their value to their families or to this nation if they were permitted to make application for citizenship after say two years rather than after five years.
I think we should look closely at the arbitrary five year requirement with a view to reducing it somewhat for persons wishing to make applications to become citizens. Whatever length of time is established it will be an arbitrary figure. There will be some fixed length of time involved. I am rather partial to a two year period or a three year period, which is approximately half that existing at the moment.
[DOT] (8:30 p.m.)
I know that in recent years there has been a tremendous influx into Canada from all parts of the world of people who have come here to settle down, raise their families and become an integral part of our nation. They are only waiting for the day when they have fulfilled the requirement of five years residence. I seriously urge the minister, in his easy and frank approach to these questions, to concern himself with this matter along with the others he has to consider. Possibly in one of his weekly or monthly statements he can tell us that the residential requirement will be reduced to something like two years or three years, admittedly an arbitrary period just as any other period would be arbitrary.
With respect to the mechanism by which a person becomes a Canadian I should like to suggest to the minister that there is a marked difference between the approach taken by the various Citizenship Courts, a marked difference in the attitude of the various judges who hear and determine applications for citizenship.
March 7, 1966

A case comes to mind of a judge we had at home who was considered so rigid and so difficult in his insistence on applicants naming all the great lakes and rivers of Canada, geographical nonsense of that kind about which many native Canadians would be uninformed, that many new Canadians refrained from making application for citizenship because they knew of the difficulties their friends and relatives had experienced when appearing before him. A change was made in the judgeship. This gentleman was moved or promoted to another post within the judicial structure. He was replaced by another judge, one who brought a kindly, gentlemanly and pleasant approach to his consideration of these applications. The approach of this second judge is the one which I think should be followed. His concern is not so much with an applicant's knowledge of the geography of the country or his ability to recite the number of provinces and so on. He is concerned about the expression of opinion and feeling on the part of the applicant. He goes further than what may be memorized; he seeks to look into an applicant's heart and mind, to find out the nature of his expectation and desire to become a Canadian citizen.
I use the example of these two judges, not naming them, to show the minister how there can be such marked, almost extreme differences in the approach taken by Citizenship Courts when considering applications. I admit at the outset that it is impossible to set down a set of rules for such cases as if one were introducing tests to determine an applicant's fitness for a driving licence. Nevertheless I believe an attempt should be made to set down guide lines or general criteria for judges in these courts to follow so that there might be some uniformity in the treatment of individuals who voluntarily make applications to become citizens with the rest of us.
These are general thoughts I pass on to the minister. They have been mentioned to many of his predecessors. I hope the present minister will remain in his post long enough to do something about them or that if he leaves he will be able so to imbue his officials with these concepts that whoever replaces him will have no choice but to carry on the policies which he has developed along these as along other lines.

I hope the humanity and understanding which the former minister showed in relation to the matters I discussed with him-I have many cases from my riding -will be continued by the present minister. The points I should like to bring to the attention of the present minister are similar to those which I drew to the attention of his predecessor. First, I do not like or appreciate in any way the policy which has been followed both by Liberals and Conservatives of permitting applications for citizenship to be denied, even after they have been recommended by the courts, without the person concerned or the member of parliament acting on his behalf being told why.
I represent, as I have said, a riding where there are a great many people of varying ethnic origins. What happens when relatives wish to visit them? What happens when sons and daughters wish to visit their parents in Canada? A visitor's visa is denied them without any explanation being given. If these people wished to become landed immigrants there might be some reason for these refusals. But when they ask only for a six month visitor's visa to see parents or other relatives whom they may not have seen for 30 years I can see no possible reason for denying them a visa and refusing to give any reason.
I am sure the present Minister of Labour, formerly minister of citizenship and immigration, knows what I have in mind. A landed immigrant who has been in Canada for five years may make a successful application for citizenship to a court. Then the authority in Ottawa says no. Surely the person concerned is entitled to know the reason for not granting citizenship in such cases and surely the

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration member of parliament who is asked to look after the case is entitled to know, even in confidence, the reason for refusal.

There are three people in my constituency whose relatives would like to get visitors' permits to see their mothers, sisters or brothers, and when the answer is no surely they are entitled to know the reason or, if necessary, their member of parliament should be given the reason in confidence. This matter has concerned me during the 13 years I have been in this chamber. It is absolutely unfair that a person should be denied citizenship after spending five years in Canada and that his relatives should also be denied the right to visit Canada on visitors' visas.
There was one case I tried to handle for five or six years. I could not get anywhere but the present Minister of Labour, when he was minister of citizenship and immigration, showed his humanity and said the persons involved should be let in and they were. I am asking that this trend be continued by the new minister or at least he should give us the reasons people are denied their rights and found guilty without the opportunity to answer the charge that must have been laid against them.

Mr. Chairman, I want to deal with Citizenship Courts first. I must echo the words of the hon. member for Skeena and say, speaking from my own experience in the Hamilton-Niagara peninsula area, that I completely agree with them. I have before me a booklet entitled "Guide to Canadian Citizenship," some 90 pages long. At the end of each chapter there is a list of questions, the answers to which an immigrant is supposed to know. In the preface it states:
When your examination takes place the judge may ask you questions on any of these subjects as a means of testing your knowledge of Canada and Canadian institutions.
At the end of each section of the booklet you will And a number of questions. The answers to many of these questions will be found in the text of the booklet. Other answers you may discover by reading or asking your friends.
That is very illuminating.
It is most important for you to understand that the questions in this booklet are not necessarily the ones that will be used by the judge in your court examination. They are simply to test your knowledge of what you have read.
And at the bottom it says "Good luck". I say that many of the people who appear before Citizenship Courts need all the luck they can get to pass the examinations because

there are some questions to which not even the Court Presidents know the answers. I tell the minister and the minister-designate that a serious look must be taken to ensure uniformity across the country concerning questions asked by Citizenship Court Presidents.
I submit that some of the qualifications of these Court Presidents are certainly not ones which fit them for the posts to which they have been appointed. If you think I am being overly harsh, Mr. Chairman, let me state that I intend to be in some respects. I have complained for three years about the Citizenship Court in my area and from personal knowledge I say a serious look must be taken at the appointments made to the presidencies of these courts.
From personal experience I know of the very arrogant approach which some Court Presidents have taken to immigrants, so arrogant that the immigrants' friends and relatives refuse to apply for citizenship because of the insults received. I know of a case where only one question was asked of the applicant but he was turned down and abused. I can understand the qualifications so far as language is concerned, but when the county court judges were handling citizenship applications we did not receive the complaints we are receiving today. Mr. Chairman, first of all I should like to congratulate the minister on his appointment to the Department of National Health and Welfare. I do not know whether this is a rest from labour or how he got this appointment but I am very glad to see him associated with this department. I was also very pleased to see the hon. lady member for Westmorland appointed as his Parliamentary Secretary and I am sure she will make a very capable assistant. This situation is all the more charming because the hon. gentleman is a bachelor. I am sure the hon. lady will help smooth out the difficult ruffles because ladies usually tend to lend a more sympathetic ear to human problems, with which the Department of National Health and Welfare is very much concerned. In all seriousness, Mr. Chairman-I have now been distracted from my speech, and am slightly embarrassed-I should like to congratulate the minister and his lovely assistant.
At this point I want to deal briefly with medicare and some of the problems inherent in it. Medicare was a plank in the Liberal platform, added very hastily and proclaimed across this country in a promise that we would have an almost universal medicare plan, 95 per cent, by 1967. In this regard I have grave doubts.
March 7, 1966	COMMONS
I am sure the minister is sincere. I have been following some of the speeches he has made outside of the house but I sometimes wonder about his success in this regard, particularly when I think back to a platform of Mackenzie King in 1919 which has as a Plank free hospitalization for Canadians. I was in the house in 1958, 39 years after that promise was made, when the Conservative government passed an Act now known as the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act. This became a fait accompli in 1958, as I say, 39 years after that promise.
I do not believe this government intends to take as long to implement their promise regarding a medicare service but I have some doubt about the 1967 target for several reasons. I do not think the way they went about this would lend itself to success. They held a meeting here in Ottawa and said they would pay the average national per capita cost of medical services across Canada at the rate of $28, but that is also the average cost in the province of Quebec. I do not even hint that Mr. Lesage was consulted in this regard, but that was not the average cost in the province of Ontario nor in many other provinces. The average cost in this province was $42 per capita, and I suggest the reason for this-this would apply to the province of British Columbia and other provinces-is that fees and para-medical services are higher. Ontario is a high cost province and I suggest it was not much wonder why Ontario and some of the other provinces did not accept this idea, particularly the province of Ontario which pays 45 per cent of taxes in Canada.
In view of these facts I am sure it is no wonder that Ontario launched its own medicare program. It is a plan that starts at a base which can be built up. This in my opinion is what is necessary in Canada in the position we find ourselves today with a shortage of doctors, para-medical services, hospital beds, research, medical schools and teachers. In my opinion it is supreme folly to say that we can have a complete medicare service in 1967. It is utterly impossible to expect such an accomplishment when one considers that the work load of general practitioners is greater than they can handle today.
I should like to suggest to the government that it take a look at what the province of Ontario has done. It has adopted a medicare scheme that will cover almost two million people. This is a plan related to Physicians Services Incorporated in the province of [DOT]Ontario which pays 90 per cent of medical

The doctor-nurse shortage would be given immediate attention by the next government following the federal election Monday.
I should like to hear from the minister as to what he has done regarding the doctor shortage.
The former minister of national health and welfare, as reported in the Canadian Press article of September 24, said:
-the goal is to have at least 95 per cent of the people of a province covered, but if that cannot be achieved initially, 90 per cent will be acceptable and there may be flexibility in the 90 per cent figure.
I suggest that both those statements contain commonsense facts.
I should now like to refer to the Hall Commission report which pointed out that there was an acute shortage of doctors, and that this plan could not be implemented at once. It pointed out that it should be started although it could not be implemented immediately because of a shortage of doctors, dentists and para-medical services. The re-

Supply-Health and Welfare port suggests, however, that this plan should be at least started. The people should not be cheated. They have been promised something and the government should go ahead with that promise. The government must start to make an effort to increase the number of doctors-not next year but now.
In this regard the government must take steps to provide four additional medical schools before 1971. We must have 500 new medical students each year in each faculty of medicine across the country. There has been a little diffidence in this regard. Some medical schools have not been able to get their quotas of students in past years. Only 7 per cent of grade 13 students is all we have been able to attract to medical faculties and that is not enough to attain the 500 new students per year which are required. I might say in this regard that we doubled the per capita grants to universities. I think in 1959.

Above all, when we get these 500 students per year it will be seven or eight years before they can be put to work in the medical field. This is not good enough. Even if the government were going to embark on medicare four years from now, they should now be creating a crash program in our medical schools, and there is no reason this cannot be done.
In 1940 a crash program was started across the land to produce doctors. The doctors were produced and medical schools were open all year round. Why should these expensive buildings and facilities remain idle during the summer months? This is a waste which at the moment we cannot afford either from the standpoint of producing doctors or cost. The minister will say we have not got the teachers to do this but we found a great many teachers between 1940 and 1945 in our forces overseas, so I suggest this would be a pretty lame excuse. In addition, through research we should be able to produce quicker and more modern methods of teaching. We could use closed circuit television in our medical schools to release teachers for research work which would make this country great. We could have special centres for special diagnostic work and information.
There is no question that we must have teachers and in this regard I think we could use some certified general practitioners. IMr. Rynard.l
When I went to medical school one of my greatest teachers was a general practitioner. I believe we could use these doctors today to get us out of this crisis, and I do not think any problem would arise. I am sure the minister is well aware that only this past month Mr. Robarts presented a report to the Ontario house from the Ontario Hospital Services Commission which stated there were not enough beds for the people who need them. This is a very serious problem and may mean that lives are lost.
The minister will probably reply that this is not his responsibility. But let me tell him that when the Conservative party came into power in 1958 it immediately doubled hospital grants for beds. Since that time nothing has been done. Our party provided for interns' quarters, for nurses' residences, for laboratories and for physiotherapy units by way of grants to each service.
I do not want to berate the minister on this subject but I would draw to his attention, because he is new to the job, that I found when I looked up the record that in the last eight years the provincial government of Ontario has increased its grants three times. Therefore I think you will agree, Mr. Chairman, that there is a serious deficiency on the part of the federal government which should be remedied at once. As I say, Ontario's government increased its grants three times, and building costs have risen from $10,000 per bed eight years ago to $20,000 to $25,000 today. During the last year I was told by an architect that hospital building costs in one city have risen 30 per cent. I am sure the minister will recognize that some of this increase is due to taxes imposed by his government.
So I just draw the attention of the minister, Mr. Chairman, to the necessity for action by way of providing beds. I would ask him whether he does not think it fair or right to plug these loopholes before embarking on a full scheme of medicare which he cannot fulfil and for which he is going to charge the people of Canada, leaving doctors overworked and patients frustrated with poor attention.

Another problem is that we have been a long way behind in many things but as we look back over the years we find that in 1951 we graduated from our medical schools 34 doctors more than were graduated in 1961 and this in spite of the fact that, excluding immigrants, there was a natural increase in population of over three million people. This is an astonishing thing. Neither governments nor universities have taken the necessary steps to correct this, and this inaction has left us in a very serious predicament. During that period of time we have had between 500 to 600 immigrant doctors per year, 90 per cent of them from the U.K. These people are well trained and a great asset. Most of them left the United Kingdom because of the introduction of state medicine and they came to this country. I should like to put on the record the fact that these doctors represent a gift of about $3 billion by way of earning power in this country over their natural lifetimes.
This money, Mr. Chairman, would build a lot of universities and schools and would provide for a lot of the research so badly needed in this country. I should also like to point out to the minister that in this country we spent last year on medical research approximately $10 million while the United States spent $1 billion. I say that is just not right. How in the world are we going to get highly qualified teachers and keep them in our universities and schools if that is all we give them for research? I hope the minister does not do this year what he did last year when he spent only 60 per cent of his budget which was approved for research purposes, leaving 40 per cent of it to go by the board. The consequence was that 40 per cent of the people who would have conducted that research were left to go to the United States or elsewhere, which is not good enough. That is why I say to the minister in a spirit of kindness that these are loopholes in his department that must be plugged.

It is a fact that 50 per cent of the hospital beds occupied in Canada today are filled by patients with mental disease. I would suggest that the government must do something to remedy this situation. The federal government should recognize support for mentally ill patients just as for physically ill patients. Are these

Mr. Chairman, I welcome the minister to his new post in the Department of National Health and Welfare and I should like to congratulate the hon. member for Westmorland on her appointment as Parliamentary Secretary to the minister. I should also like to join with the minister in the tribute that he paid to the efficient and hard working staff -that he has in his department. I have been around here now for a few years and I have got to know a few civil servants. It happens because of the committees I have been on and particular interests I have had that I have got to know the members of his staff, and the work that -they do in a special way. I want to say that in my view his tribute to the work they do was well deserved.
I said at the outset that I welcomed the minister to his new department. I am sure that he will not be surprised if I remind him that in the department he left, he left behind a number of items of unfinished business. I will not recite them now because it would be out of order to do so. I recited them the other night when the estimates of the Department of Labour were before us. However, he is already aware of the fact that, if he left behind some items of unfinished business, he

inherited some when he came into the Department of National Health and Welfare. I do not detract for a moment from the good job that his predecessor did, with a little help of course, in getting the Canada Pension Plan onto the statute books. However, there were a few items that even she was not able to accomplish in the last parliament.
Mainly, what I want to do in these few minutes in which I now choose to speak is to remind the minister of these items and to urge him to get cracking on them.
First of all, and I say this briefly because my colleague, the hon. member for Van-couver-Kingsway will deal with this as well as other matters in greater detail, he must not ever get the notion that the old age security pension can be left where it is, at $75 a month. The fact that this house made a decision the wrong way on a couple of motions earlier in this session does not settle the issue so far as the Canadian people are concerned. All the arguments that were used last session to the effect that the pension package would have been a better one if we had matched the Canada Pension Plan with $100 a month as the old age security pension not only still stand but are given greater force by the increase in the cost of living which has taken place since that time.
I urge the minister to realize that he simply must cope with this issue. It is just as urgent a matter as were the important matters that he had to deal with when he was Minister of Labour.

I was listening carefully. That was one of the points the hon. member made, and I made a note of it because I wanted to draw attention to the inconsistency of telling the government it was 10 years behind the times and then urging it to slow down, to wait another 10 years or another 47.
I want to say what hardly needs to be said because it is a principle which has been recognized time and time again and it has been documented extremely well in the Hall report-that in this field of medicare there is no room for any kind of means test such as one finds in the plan which has been brought into effect in this province. In the Ontario plan a division is made between those who have one level of income and those who have another, thereby introducing into this important social legislation a basis of discrimination which will before long, I believe, prove just as damaging to the dignity of human beings as the means test was for the many years when it was applied to determine eligibility for old age pensions.
I urge the minister to face the fact that precisely because Ontario and other provinces have come along with inferior plans is no reason for the federal government to go slowly. On the contrary, this is all the more reason for the federal government to move faster. Indeed, the fact that some of the provinces have come in with other plans underlines the mistake which has been made by the federal government in delaying. Had action only been taken in this area a long time ago we should be a lot better off.
Speaking of the hon. member for Simcoe East and inconsistencies on his part to which I wanted to draw attention, I note he complained because Mr. King delayed for so
March 7, 1966

Supply-Health and Welfare many years with regard to hospitalization as one aspect of national insurance-delayed and delayed until it was left to a Conservative government to implement the first hospital insurance plan. I think that for the record it should be pointed out that the Liberals brought in the legislation just before they were defeated in 1957 but it took the Conservatives to make the necessary amendments so that the legislation could be implemented.
The hon. member complained that Mr. King was so slow. But tonight he employs the very arguments that we used to hear from Mr. King. He used to tell us it was no use having hospital insurance until we had the hospital beds. Now, tonight, the hon. member who condemns Mr. King is saying it is no use having medicare until we have all the doctors and all the facilities necessary for carrying it out. I suggest that one of the things which led to an increase in the number of hospital beds and to the building of hospitals was precisely the growth of hospital insurance and I contend that the same would happen in the field of medicare. I urge the government not to retreat by one iota from the four points the Prime Minister laid down in July, 1965. Personally, and speaking for this party, I would like to see the Hall report implemented in full. But at least those four points which the Prime Minister laid down last July are good and provide a basis for a good medicare scheme in this country. Let me repeat them.
First, it was proposed that the contribution by the present government to provincial schemes would require that coverage in the province be universal; second, that the coverage would take into account the broad range of medical needs required; third, that the plan should be government operated; fourth, that the plan should be portable among the provinces of Canada. I suggest that nothing less than this is good enough and I urge that action on this kind of plan be taken during the present session.
The hon. member for Simcoe East, drawing attention to the change which had to be made in the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act, reminded us of the fact that the Liberal government of the St. Laurent day stood for a long time on the position that it would not move into hospital insurance until a certain number of the provinces representing a certain portion of the population would enter this field. For some time the present government was taking a similar position with regard to medicare. Recently, however, 
the government has moved away from that position, and I hope it stays away from it.
What the government should do now, I strongly suggest, is to bring in this legislation, put it on the statute books and make it available to the provinces as they are prepared to come in, even if there are only two or three provinces at first. That is the only way in which hospital insurance got going and I suggest it is the only way in which medicare will get going. I am glad to get the minister's attention at this point. I urge him to take action on these lines. I hope he will not take the position that with the hon. member for Simcoe East urging him to go in one direction and the member for Winnipeg North Centre urging him to go in another, he can try to go down the middle. There is no middle way between a means test and universality; there is no middle way between a partial plan and full coverage. We suggest that if the government is worth its salt this is the area in which it must act during this session. I know that the minister and the former parliamentary secretary to the department, the hon. member for Hamilton East-the present parliamentary secretary has not been there long enough-do not like being reminded of the years, the decades, the eons of time it has taken to get action out of this government. We are talking about things which were started before those three, the see no evil, speak no evil, hear no evil trio over there, were even born. This is a fact we have had to live with, the myth that the Liberals would move in the direction of social progress.
[DOT] (9:50 p.m.)
The Canadian people have had to assume that because the Liberals were in power they were getting things that they were not getting at all. We think the time has gone for the Canadian people to be asked to live under that myth and that the time has come for action in this terribly important field of medicare.
The minister does not need to worry about the unfinished business he left behind in the Department of Labour. A new minister can take that on, but he has some pretty important items in this department upon which I hope he will act. I urge him to do so without delay.

But, we, as legislators, must recognize that the cost of living, for our Canadian families, is not the same thing in 1966 as it was in 1950 or in 1945 either.
We voted for the motions for an increase for our aged people in Canada. We want family allowances to be related to the cost-of-living index.
In other areas, we frequently have to call on the Department of National Health and Welfare for subsidies to cultural centres in our section of the province. In this connection, the minister is not too much in a hurry. I understand that he has switched to another department. He did a wonderful job in the Department of Labour and I hope he will do the same in his new department.
Cultural centres exist not only in Montreal, Ottawa, Toronto, Winnipeg or Vancouver. Other parts of the province and of the country require the same attention from the federal authorities. And the hon. minister is surely conscious of those needs or, at least, we are bringing them to his attention.
Then, he must give us answers or try to do the impossible so that our constituencies may get a fair treatment.
Another point to which the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) just called the minister's attention is the
Supply-Health and Welfare famous medicare plan that for many years members of the New Democratic Party have been clamouring for and which was set up in Saskatchewan with great difficulty because of the manifold and real obstacles brought about by common sense and then, they had to change their mind.
What we suggest as a Canadian medical plan is called the health dividend. Instead of the government setting up a government insurance company which would employ doctors and tell them how to treat sick and disabled persons in Canada, or persons in need of a medical plan, we suggest that the government should issue a national health voucher to every Canadian family.
It could be $150 per family and from $90 to $100 per bachelor in the country. With this voucher, the Canadian citizen, family head or bachelor, could select his insurance company, the medical plans or plan already in existence. It can already be secured through private industry, from any insurance company, the Artisans canadiens frangais, The Canada Life, The Crown Life, The Mutual Life, The Sun Life, it doesn't matter which; all these companies are organized to assure people and provide them with medical insurance. It is available in group insurance.

I hear the hon. member for York South say: "for profit motives". When the hon. member for York South needs a doctor, he is not concerned with the doctors' profits, because when he wants a doctor, it is the doctor he is interested in and not the doctor's profits. He is concerned with the care the doctor can give him.
It is natural for companies to make profits. When enthusiasm and initiative are taken away in a society, we retrogress instead of progressing. That is exactly what the member for York South wants to do; that is exactly what is happening in Russia, which we visited last year.
Mr. Chairman, that is not what we want. I think that the citizen should have freedom of choice with regard to medical insurance. He chooses the plan he wants; he chooses his doctor. That is what is important in a democracy: to give citizens freedom of choice.
The plan which we suggest, the health dividend, would mean insurance jor all citizens. It would cost the government about 35 to 40 per cent less than medicare or a national health insurance plan in Canada.

And that is what the people from the New Democratic Party and the social democratic party, or the socialist parties of Canada, cannot understand. What matters to them is that the government controls the individual in his home, in society, everywhere. This is not what we want. We want the individual to remain independent, people to be respected, and in order to give them that respect and security, they must have the financial means which to choose what they want, because it is the human being himself who has to determine what must be done and what is good for him. It does not rest with the government to do that for him. Let us respect that freedom.

Mr. Speaker, last week, in terms which are quite in fashion these days, I put the following question to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Greene):
As the new dairy year is starting in a few days, is the minister in a position to tell us where we stand in the count-down before the launching or the placing into orbit of the new dairy policy which is intended to guarantee Canadian milk producers a minimum price of $4 per hundredweight for industrial milk?
Mr. Speaker, you know that the dairy industry in eastern Canada is of vital significance to the farm economy of this country, and particularly to our farmers and dairy producers. We also know that dairy producers in the eastern section of this country are most anxious to hear about this new policy which was supposed to be announced very soon.
Tonight, I shall try to give the hon. parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Beer) the dates on which the dairy policies were announced since 1958-59.
During those years the dairy year began on May 1, but we all know that last year, the former Minister of Agriculture anticipated by one month the start of the dairy year 1965-66.
For the year 1958-59, the new dairy policy was announced on April 7. For the year starting May 1, for the period 1959-60, the policy was announced on April 23; for the year 1960-61, which started on May 1, the policy was announced on April 13.
In 1961, the policy was announced on April 20, for the year 1961-62 starting on May 1.

In 1962, the policy was announced on March 22. It was revised on April 9, 1962, and on April 27, the policy for the dairy year 1962-63 was again revised.
In 1963, the policy for the dairy year starting May 1 was announced on April 29, and it will be remembered that, on that occasion, hon. members representing rural counties had received numerous petitions and protests from dairy producers who had been informed of the new dairy policy only a few hours before the new dairy year.
In 1963, we could expect a late date, because a general election had been held on April 8 and the minister had just then been appointed. But in 1964, the policy was announced on April 29, a few hours before the new dairy year, that is on May 1.
Last year the policy was announced on March 26, and this was an improvement, although it was announced a month and a few days before the beginning of the new dairy year. In spite of that, last year protests were raised against the policy and we could read in the Canadian press, more especially in the Terre de Chez Nous, some editorials of this kind:
After enticing but vague promises will there be disappointing and harsh facts?
Mr. Speaker, I am interested tonight, as are all hon. members and especially the dairy producers, in knowing-and I think the Parliamentary Secretary will be in a position to give us an idea-when the dairy policy for the new year will be announced in the house, so that we may discuss it and make our proposals before it is brought into force.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank the hon. members for directing his question concerning the dairy policy of the government to me at this particular time. He mentioned that he was patiently awaiting the introduction of the new dairy policy of the government. I can readily understand why he would be patiently awaiting the new dairy policy of this government and permit me to review briefly the dairy policy which has been in effect.
The government has had four main objectives for its dairy policy: First, to balance production and consumption; second, to remove the surplus of butter which existed when this government took office, a surplus of some 239 million pounds; third, to increase the production of cheese for which there was

It will be the objective of this government to see that farmers receive a maximum price for their milk at the farm of something about the $3.50 level. This is our aim. I can only tell the hon. member at this particular time that the policy will be announced by the minister in due course. I am sure he awaits it with anticipation and will greet it with great satisfaction.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the fact that I am grand marshal of the Irishmen's parade this year and that tonight I am speaking about D'Arcy McGee is no coincidence. In this day of communication I think the average youngster is more familiar with the exploits of Davey Crockett than he is with La Verendrye, Radisson, LaSalle and other men whose careers were much more exciting than Davey Crockett's. I think it is safe to say that most high school students are more familiar with the assassination of Abraham Lincoln than they are with the assassination of one of the Fathers of Confederation, Thomas D'Arcy McGee. He was assassinated by a Fenian known as Whelan.
Thomas D'Arcy McGee was first elected to parliament in 1858 as an independent, sponsored at that time by the St. Patrick Society. In a moment of weakness he became a Conservative and it has taken the Irish almost 98 years to forget that blemish on his character.
On the day that Thomas D'Arcy McGee was buried in Montreal one of the largest funerals in Canadian history took place, which is a tribute to the fine relationship that existed between the Irish and French speaking Montrealers. The funeral took place first at St. Patrick's Cathedral and then proceeded

The tombstone that marks his resting place was, to the best of the knowledge of the historians of the Montreal area, paid for by a family named Wilson and has been maintained through the years by the St. Patrick Society of Montreal. That society has informed me that his tombstone, because of the type of stone used almost 100 years ago, has reached the point where it should be replaced in a fitting manner.
I notice the Minister of Trade and Commerce is in the chamber. Although I am a great supporter of Expo '67, I think in the final analysis our centennial celebration will be of more lasting benefit to Canada than Expo '67. I would therefore urge the Secretary of State that as one of our centennial achievements the federal government should absorb the cost of providing a suitable tombstone for the grave of Thomas D'Arcy McGee. I realize that the Parliamentary Secretary will probably tell me that the proper procedure is for the city of Montreal to sponsor this, with the federal government paying a portion of the cost. I immediately must state that the memory of Thomas D'Arcy McGee does not belong to Montreal and does not belong to the St. Patrick Society. That memory is not the exclusive property of the Irish Canadians of this country but belongs to all Canadians. He was a Father of Confederation and as such I think the federal government has a duty and, in many ways, a privilege to provide a tombstone for the grave of Thomas D'Arcy McGee as a part of our centennial celebrations next year.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Verdun (Mr. Mac-kasey) certainly deserves our congratulations and our admiration for having recalled, on the eve of the centennial of the Confederation, and carried away by his patriotism, the memory of one of the most brilliant speakers of our Parliamentary history, a polished writer and a fine poet, a great administrator, one of the Fathers of Confederation:	Thomas
D'Arcy McGee, born in the green Erin. My hon. friend's plea comes very appropriately just in time to support a recent request made by the Saint Patrick's Society of Montreal.
The hon. member may be pleased to learn that under a federal-provincial program of

per capita grants sponsored by the centennial commission, funds are available for carrying out the type of project he proposes. However, under this program, all requests must first be approved by the provinces and then obtain the approval of the centennial commission.
In the present case, it is not presumptuous to state that the commission would look with favour upon such a request. In fact, the centennial commission recently received a similar project from the Prince Edward Island authorities and it is about to grant its approval.
In closing, may I remind my hon. colleague that a project exists which was announced in 1964 by the Boy Scouts of Canada, with the financial assistance of the centennial commission. Under this project, the boy scouts are responsible for inspecting the tombs of all the Fathers of Confederation, for reporting in what condition they are and for undertaking to restore them if need be.
Once that work is finished, the boy scouts will lay wreaths during the year 1967 and organize ceremonies to which will be invited all the descendants of the Fathers of Confederation, to whom we owe our constitution.

subtopic: COMMUNIQUE FOLLOWING JOINT CANADA-U.S. MINISTERIAL MEETING

speechtext:
The Tenth Meeting of the Joint United States-Canadian Committee on Trade and Economic Affairs was held in Washington, D.C., March 4-5, 1966.
As background to the discussions on trade and economic matters, the United States Secretary of State and the Canadian Secretary of State for External Affairs reviewed, major recent international developments.
The Committee exchanged views on current developments in the closely related economies of the two countries, noting with satisfaction that both had achieved a record of sustained economic expansion unparalleled in their histories and they looked forward to another year of strong growth. They recognized, however, that maintaining price and cost stability will require close and continuing attention.
The Committee discussed the balance of payments of both countries. They recognized that decisive progress had been made toward reducing the United States balance of payments deficit and reviewed the measures being taken to bring the United States external accounts into balance. In this connection, the Committee noted the measures that have been taken to maintain access to the United States capital market for an unlimited amount of new Canadian securities free of the Interest Equalization Tax. The United States members reaffirmed that, in buying such issues, U.S. investors were completely free to be guided by market considerations.
Canadian Ministers expressed their concern over the possible implications for Canada of the United States voluntary program on direct investment and the relation of this program to the position of Canadian subsidiaries of U.S. corporations. The United States members made clear that the U.S. Government was not requesting U.S. corporations to induce their Canadian subsidiaries to act in any ways that differed from their normal business practices as regards the repatriation of earnings, purchasing and sales policies, or their other financial and commercial activities. United States members re-emphasized the view that United States subsidiaries abroad should behave as good citizens of the country
where they are located. Where U.S. companies were in doubt as to these views, the U.S. Government would ensure that any misunderstandings would be dispelled.
The Canadian Ministers expressed serious concern that proposed Securities and Exchange Commission regulations would subject to United States law Canadian companies not deliberately seeking to sell securities in the United States if their shares had happened to be purchased by United States residents. These regulations, moreover, would discriminate against Canadian companies by imposing more severe requirements relative to other foreign companies. Canadian Ministers referred to plans under way in Canada to improve the disclosure of information regarding Canadian enterprises and the regulation of the issue of securities. They strongly urged that the United States authorities refrain from applying these SEC regulations to Canadian companies which do not seek to sell their securities in the United States. The United States members appreciated the concern of the Government of Canada and assured the Canadian members that the most careful consideration would be given to Canadian views in an effort to work out at an early date mutually satisfactory arrangements.
The Committee discussed United States foreign assets controls as they may affect the exports of companies in Canada. The United States members reaffirmed their readiness to consult promptly on any transactions of importance to Canada which are affected by United States foreign assets control. They also stated that regulations over exports of technical data are being revised and that, in light of the Committee's discussions, further consideration will be given to the possibilities of additional modifications of the regulations.
The Committee discussed a number of specific bilateral trade and financial matters on both sides, including Canadian Cheddar cheese and Canadian oil exports to the United States, and agreed to keep them under review. The Committee agreed that a joint examination should be made of trade in agricultural implements, tractors, and aircraft for which tariff liberalization would be most important.

They agreed that the removal of unnecessary restrictions on the free flow of goods and services across the border would contribute importantly to the continued prosperity of both countries. The Committee recognized that the Automotive Agreement represents a long stride toward free trade in a basic industry of major importance to the two countries and had resulted in a substantial increase in two-way trade to the benefit of production and employment both in Canada and the United States. Greater benefits are to be expected as industry in both countries adjust their operations to take full advantage of the opportunities afforded by the Agreement.
In the area of international economic relations, the Committee agreed that the Kennedy Round negotiations in Geneva provided an unparalleled opportunity for the substantial liberalization of world trade, which would benefit all participating countries -developing as well as developed. The Committee, therefore, concluded that the highest priority must be given to the timely completion of these negotiations which are now entering their critical phase. They agreed that the Canadian and U.S. delegations would continue to work closely together in the interest of a successful conclusion of the Kennedy Round negotiations, including the negotiation of a world cereals agreement in which the two North American exporting countries have a strong common interest.
The Committee reviewed the trade and development problems of the developing countries particularly in food and agriculture. They noted the food needs in India and the steps being taken by the Indian Government to deal with the problem. Although both countries were providing assistance to India and other developing countries, they noted that more would be needed during the period ahead from other countries. The Canadian members informed the Committee of Canada's recent decision to make available to India a substantially larger amount of food aid.
The Committee discussed the consultative arrangements between the two Governments in the light of the Heeney-Merchant report and agreed on the importance of close and
effective working relationships between the two Governments.
The Committee took note of the importance of the work on improving the international monetary system being undertaken by the International Monetary Fund and the Deputies of the Group of Ten. They expressed the hope that the Deputies will be able to reach agreement on a constructive report to the Ministers, which would permit further negotiations on a broader basis.
The Ministers noted with concern the serious problem of pollution of Lake Erie, Lake Ontario and the international section of the St. Lawrence River, as described in the recent Interim Report to the Canadian and the United States Governments by the International Joint Commission. They recorded their support for the recommendations in the report and agreed that efforts in both countries should be coordinated to deal with this problem as a matter of urgency.
